Regional Perspectives on the House of Assad’s Fall | International Crisis Group

Newspaper front-pages headline the fall of Syrian president Bashar al-Assad's rule, in Tehran, on December 9, 2024. Tehran, Iran. ATTA KENARE / AFP

 Commentary / Middle East & North Africa 17 December 2024 20+ minutes 

# Regional Perspectives on the House of Assad’s Fall 

The Assad dynasty’s demise will certainly remake Syria, but it will also reshape relations between Damascus and other capitals. Crisis Group experts offer a 360-degree view of how the Syrian crisis could shake up regional politics.

The crisis leading to President Bashar al-Assad’s ouster from Syria began as a popular uprising in 2011. It then became a bloody civil war enveloped in a proxy conflict involving a number of external players. Over the ensuing thirteen years, prominent outside interventions came from Gulf Arab states, Hizbollah, Iran, Iraqi armed groups, Israel, Russia, Türkiye and the United States. Yet, in the end, it was mainly Syrians themselves who overthrew the Assad regime, with the rebel group Hei’at Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), led by Abu Mohammed al-Jolani (or Ahmed al-Sharaa, who has now shed his nom de guerre), playing a central role. The Assad family fled to Russia, where they received asylum, while in Damascus al-Sharaa set out on the task of building a new governing authority. How he will do so in such a big, diverse and politically pluralistic country, with many armed factions that might contend for power and a conflict under way in the north east, is the open question Syria now faces. 

Syria’s immediate neighbours and interested powers from farther afield, including Russia and the U.S., are watching intently to see how HTS, a former al-Qaeda affiliate, governs – and whether reports of its moderation turn out to be accurate or aspirational. Many are concerned that the country may descend back into factional fighting if the informal understandings made among armed groups after the regime’s demise break down. Some are reaching out to open lines of communication with HTS; others are striking quick-fix deals to protect their interests; and others – particularly Türkiye, Israel and the U.S. – are also using military force to address perceived threats and advance their interests. In repeated aerial attacks since 8 December, Israel has destroyed an estimated 70-80 per cent of Syria’s military capability, while a Turkish proxy is battling a U.S.-backed Kurdish-dominated militia in the north east, which is creating a new humanitarian emergency. Against this backdrop, Crisis Group experts offer the following brief survey of the discussions in various capitals about the latest developments. 

## Türkiye

The Assad regime was a longstanding Turkish adversary, and its collapse presents Ankara with both opportunities and challenges. The shift of power away from Assad’s erstwhile allies Russia and Iran – both of which Türkiye competes with for Middle East influence – gives Ankara a chance to enhance its sway in Syria. Ankara has had pragmatic engagement with HTS for years, forging ties that could now help it steer the new authorities in Damascus in a direction to its liking. The regime’s fall could also pave the way for large numbers of Syrian refugees living in Türkiye to go home, offering the Turkish government relief from what was becoming a political headache and a drain on the country’s resources. But these developments have not resolved what Ankara deems its main security concern – the quasi-autonomous enclave in north-eastern Syria ruled by the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), a group that helped the U.S. defeat ISIS. The SDF’s dominant component is the People’s Protection Units, which has connections to the Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK), which Türkiye, the U.S. and the EU have designated as a terrorist group. The big questions are now how Ankara’s relationship with HTS will evolve and how both Türkiye and the former rebels will deal with the SDF.

When Ankara first got wind of the planned rebel offensive, it counselled caution. Turkish officials worried that an assault would avail the rebels little, while prompting a regime and Russian counterattack that would send still more refugees streaming into Türkiye. They say they warned the rebels not to attack the regime’s lines, but it became clear the rebels would do so anyway. At that point, Ankara may have acquiesced, thinking that the offensive would not get very far or that it might accomplish an intermediary outcome: pressing Damascus to negotiate with the Syrian opposition, consistent with Türkiye’s preference for a weakened, but not destroyed, Assad regime. Ankara was caught off guard by the rebels’ rapid progress all the way to Damascus, but it moved quickly to signal its support for the new order. Türkiye’s intelligence chief, Ibrahim Kalın, made a public appearance in Damascus four days after the regime fell. On 14 December, Türkiye reopened its embassy in the Syrian capital, which it had closed in 2012.

 Türkiye is well positioned to assist the new Syria, economically and politically. Turkish companies are poised to play a role in rebuilding the country. 

Türkiye is well positioned to assist the new Syria, economically and politically. Turkish companies are poised to play a role in rebuilding the country, as suggested by the surge in Turkish construction and cement companies’ stocks the day after the regime’s collapse. Ankara could also help ease frictions among competing rebel factions, and its officials are already encouraging HTS to share power with other opposition groups, including Türkiye’s proxy, the Syrian National Army (SNA). On 10 December, President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan expressed his hope that Syria’s new leadership would adopt an inclusive approach that embraced all segments of Syrian society.

The decisive factor in Ankara’s relationship with the new Syria will be developments in the north east. For eight years, Türkiye has been carrying out offensives against the SDF, conducting airstrikes on SDF positions and mobilising troops stationed in parts of northern Syria along the 911km border. Its long-time objective has been to prevent the PKK (which it sees as inseparable from the SDF) from creating a statelet in north-eastern Syria.

But Ankara is constrained in this project by the U.S.-led counter-ISIS coalition forces that remain in the north east, and SNA units are already using the country’s shifting dynamics to try breaking the deadlock. Since the rebels’ advance began, SNA forces have driven the SDF from Tal Rifaat and Manbij, two important towns in the region, and are now heading toward Kobani, where the SDF (with U.S. support) famously fought off an ISIS siege in 2015. It is unclear whether U.S. leverage over the SDF and Ankara will translate into a successful effort to nudge them toward an accommodation.

## Iran

The Assad regime’s collapse capped months of setbacks for the Islamic Republic’s regional strategy. In September, Israel stepped up its campaign against Hizbollah in Lebanon, Tehran’s most important non-state partner in the “axis of resistance” network. In October, an exchange of strikes and counter-strikes with Israel exposed gaps in Iran’s air defences and dented its missile production. The announcement of a ceasefire in Lebanon in late November might have provided Iran with a reprieve to regroup and contain the damage. But the lightning rebel offensive in Syria quickly rendered that possibility moot, defenestrating in less than two weeks an ally for whose survival Tehran had sacrificed blood, treasure and reputation over many years.

As Iranian officials tell it, Assad’s fate was sealed by his own foibles: he presided over a rotting state, guarded by a military that, when pressed, mounted no serious defence on his behalf. As rebel forces swiftly gained ground, neither Iran nor its partners stepped into the breach. It is hard to know whether they stayed out because they faced operational constraints in dispatching additional arms and troops or because they saw little point in trying to rescue an ally whose own armed forces seemed already to have conceded the fight. It may have been a mix of both.

Assad’s fall not only deprives the Islamic Republic of a longstanding state ally, but it also renders more challenging plans to rebuild Hizbollah’s diminished military capabilities through Syria – a conduit regularly in Israeli crosshairs. The supply corridors in Iran’s “forward defence” doctrine, once central to its efforts to project power and deter adversaries, have been dealt a severe below. Although Iran’s government has reportedly been in contact with Syria’s new HTS-led authorities, al-Sharaa’s comment that the Assad regime made Syria “a playground for Iranian ambitions” suggests a low ceiling for relations in the near term and leaves Iran in a bind. Should a future Syrian government fragment, Tehran might hope to exploit the rifts. But in the meantime, it faces a short-term challenge in how to maintain access to Lebanon and its Hizbollah partners.

 The combined hammering of Hamas, Hizbollah and Assad over the past fourteen months has laid bare the problems with Iran’s regional vision. 

More fundamentally, the combined hammering of Hamas, Hizbollah and Assad over the past fourteen months has laid bare the problems with Iran’s regional vision. Yet the debate in Tehran is mostly framed around apportioning responsibility for failure, rather than any consideration of a new path forward. Officials are arguing about whether Assad deserves all the blame for underestimating the machinations of Iran’s adversaries or, in the view of some hardliners, whether the Iranian government should get some, too, for what they consider its timidity in countering Israeli strikes at home and abroad. Domestically, moderate and reformist politicians point to Assad’s downfall as a cautionary tale about what can happen when a widening gap between state and society undermines regime stability – hinting that something similar could lie in store for Iran. In remarks on 11 December, Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei maintained that “the more pressure you exert, the stronger the resistance becomes. … Iran is strong and powerful – and will become even stronger”. But the trend of recent months belies that message. 

## Israel

For Israel, the Assad regime’s removal from Syria presents both opportunities and risks. The regime’s departure is another blow to Iran, Israel’s primary regional foe, and the “axis of resistance” through which Iran tried to harry Israel by proxy while shielding itself from Israeli attack. Crucially for Israel, Syria is no longer a reliable conduit that Tehran can use to supply its Lebanese partner, Hizbollah. At the same time, Israel had come to rely on Assad to prevent Iran-backed militias from launching attacks on Israel from the parts of the Golan Heights under Syrian control. Now, two unpredictable elements are in the mix: the rise of HTS, a Sunni Islamist group, to at least temporary power in Damascus and the growth of Türkiye’s influence. These changes have prompted Israel to take some matters into its own hands.

Some of its focus has been on the Golan Heights, a portion of which Israel occupied in the 1967 war and later annexed. (The Trump administration recognised Israel’s annexation in 2019 and the Biden administration has maintained that position. Most of the rest of world still considers the Golan to be occupied territory.) In 1974, the U.S. brokered an agreement whereby the Syrian army would withdraw from an area at most about 8km wide to the east and north east of the Israeli-occupied Golan. Since then, calm has largely prevailed on that front, but Assad’s fall raised concerns within the Israeli government. In the ensuing chaos, officials thought, rebels and other hostile groups might advance south west and pose a threat to Golan settlers.
